extracted.intended_audience: independent inventors, startup founders, and people preparing a patent application
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for planning and executing a comprehensive patent prior art search to assess novelty, non-obviousness, and freedom-to-operate before filing. Covers strategy, tools, sources (patent and non-patent), analysis steps, and when to engage professionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make prior art search the first step
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent prior art search is the single most important first step an inventor can take to see if their idea has a real shot at becoming a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't 'jump into the patent process' without a thorough prior art search — it can reveal roadblocks early and save time and legal fees. Treat the search as the foundation of your IP strategy that affects claim drafting and examiner negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include non-patent literature (NPL)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art is not limited to existing patents; it can be almost anything publicly available (academic papers, product manuals, marketing brochures, conference presentations, blog posts, YouTube videos).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single scientific paper or obscure product manual can invalidate novelty. Search scholarly databases, conference proceedings, white papers, trade magazines, archived websites, and manuals as part of the search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search globally (do not limit to U.S. patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: A search limited to only U.S. patents is dangerously incomplete — major collections like the EPO contain global technical documents and often cite non-U.S. prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dig deep into global patent databases; use international databases and be aware that critical prior art may be published outside the U.S. and in other languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deconstruct the invention to build a search strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe your invention in a single, clear sentence and then pull that sentence apart into key nouns, verbs, technical terms, functions, and the problem it solves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brainstorm synonyms, alternative phrases, and related concepts for every key term (example: 'solar-powered automatic pet feeder' -> feeder, solar panel, timer, dispenser, synonyms, functional language). Use an invention disclosure format to generate a rich vocabulary for search queries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and focus on the point of novelty (inventive concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pinpoint the core unique mechanism, process, or combination of parts that makes the invention new and non-obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus searches on that 'point of novelty' to avoid thousands of irrelevant results and to craft sophisticated queries that hunt for concepts rather than product names or marketing language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use patent classification systems (CPC) in addition to keywords
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent classification (e.g., Cooperative Patent Classification - CPC) organizes inventions by technical features and is essential to finding patents that use different words to describe similar technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find CPC codes from a similar patent and use them to search databases directly; combine CPC codes with keyword lists for a two-pronged approach that reduces noise and increases relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use effective search tools and Boolean/operators
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with free platforms like Google Patents and the USPTO Patent Public Search (PPUBS) and use advanced search operators (AND, OR, NOT) and filters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example Boolean query: (solar OR photovoltaic) AND (pet AND feeder) NOT cat. Use 'find prior art' features, search by patent number/inventor, and mine 'References Cited' to follow examiner-identified relevant documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: When stakes are high, use professional subscription and AI-driven platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Subscription platforms (PatSnap, IPRally, Amplified, Derwent Innovation) provide semantic/AI search, analytics, global patent families, and advanced dashboards for deeper, concept-based searching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hybrid approach is recommended: begin with free tools, then invest in professional services if the invention's complexity/value justifies the expense. AI semantic search can surface conceptually similar patents that keyword searches miss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search specialized academic and technical databases
rubrics_metrics.description: For many fields, especially electronics, computer science, and biomedical, scholarly databases are indispensable prior art sources (IEEE Xplore, Google Scholar, PubMed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same conceptual keyword / CPC strategies in these databases; use 'cited by' features to follow research trails and identify older foundational disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search commercial and archived sources for product disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial materials — product manuals, marketing brochures, archived websites, and out-of-print trade magazines — can be prior art even if no product was ever commercialized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tools like the Wayback Machine to find old product pages and PDFs. Remember that disclosure, not commercial success or functionality, is what counts as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break the language barrier (translate foreign documents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Important prior art may be published in other languages (German, Japanese, Korean, etc.), so searches must include foreign-language documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use built-in machine translation features in major patent databases for initial triage; for critical documents, consider professional translation to confirm relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiently triage and read patent documents (drawings → abstract → specification → claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: You don't need to read every word; start with figures for visual similarity, then read the abstract, scan the detailed description, and finally analyze the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This staged approach lets you quickly discard irrelevant documents and focus detailed attention only on the references that appear relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissect claims element-by-element to check for anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims are the legally enforceable core; compare each claim of a prior art document, element-by-element, against the elements of your invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a prior art claim discloses every element of one of your proposed claims, that claim is anticipated (novelty destroyed). Perform detailed, feature-by-feature comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess obviousness by considering combinations of references
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if no single reference anticipates your invention, examiners may combine multiple references to argue obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether combining the references would make the inventive leap 'a simple, logical next step' to a person of ordinary skill in the art; be brutally honest in this analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify dates to confirm prior art status
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm that the publication or filing date of each reference is before your invention date or relevant priority date so it legally qualifies as prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Date verification is essential to ensure a reference can be used to challenge novelty or obviousness; document effective dates carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a consistent checklist for analyzing each reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow a structured process for each flagged reference: initial review, detailed comparison, claim dissection, obviousness check, and date verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document why a reference was disqualified or kept. A consistent checklist ensures thoroughness and prevents emotional or ad-hoc decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when your search is 'good enough' (point of diminishing returns)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art search is never 100% complete; the finish line is when additional searches keep returning the same handful of key references and further digging is unlikely to change the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to shrink uncertainty to a manageable level rather than absolute certainty. Stop when different search angles converge on the same results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide between self-search and hiring professionals (hybrid approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: You should do a preliminary search yourself using free tools, but for a comprehensive professional-level search, hire a patent attorney or specialized search firm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professionals add access to subscription databases and advanced search expertise; a hybrid workflow (self triage → professional deep dive) often yields the best cost-benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the difference: novelty (patentability) search vs freedom-to-operate (FTO) search
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelty/patentability search looks at everything ever published to determine if you can get a patent; an FTO search looks only at active, in-force patents in a specific country to determine legal freedom to commercialize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use novelty search to answer 'Can I get a patent?' and FTO to answer 'Can I sell my product without getting sued?'; choose scope and databases accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turn search analysis into strategy (pivot, design-around, proceed, or consider alternatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use your findings not just as a yes/no on patentability but as a strategic roadmap: abandon/pivot on 'knockout' references, design around close references, proceed if only distant art exists, or consider trade secrets/first-to-market if field is crowded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document how findings affect claim drafting, patent valuation, and commercial/IP strategy. The analysis informs whether to modify the invention, pursue protection, or adopt a non-patent strategy.
